Researcher Joanna Martin says validated tools to study masking are being developed, while warning against treating unvalidated social-media checklists as evidence. The government’s review of ADHD, autism and mental health diagnoses is expected to address the wider rise in diagnoses, but the article says its precise scope remains unclear.

content.headline: Hotter, drier UK summers may push growers towards different crops
content.shortHeadline: Climate pressures put alternative UK crops on the table
content.standfirst: Researchers are testing crops such as lupins, chickpeas and lablab as heat and drought challenge familiar harvests. Their future role is uncertain: yields, suitable growing regions, pests and late frosts all need further investigation.

image.caption: A lupin bhaji made with flour from an alternative crop being tested for UK growing conditions.

sources.originalTitle: The protein-packed superfoods of the future – that you could grow in your garden

segments.body: After a hot, dry summer affected garden and farm yields, researchers at Southampton University are investigating crops that could cope better with warmer, drier conditions. Lupins, chickpeas and lablab are among the possibilities; lupin flour is relatively high in protein, while chickpeas are drought tolerant. Researchers stress that edible lupins are different from ornamental garden varieties, which cannot be eaten without processing.

segments.title: No guaranteed winners
segments.body: The researchers say more work is needed to establish which UK regions and varieties suit crops such as chickpeas, and to assess disease and pest risks. The Royal Horticultural Society’s Guy Barter expects some varieties to do better further north, while warning that warmer-climate fruit trees may still be vulnerable to late spring frosts. Climate change may create opportunities for some growers, but the winners and losers remain uncertain.

content.headline: Judge calls warrantless Flock searches ‘indiscriminate mass surveillance’
content.shortHeadline: US judge questions warrantless Flock searches
content.standfirst: A federal judge ruled that a Tulsa sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s rights by searching a license-plate database without a warrant. The decision is not binding precedent, but adds to scrutiny of automated plate-reader networks.

sources.originalTitle: Federal judge calls Flock ‘indiscriminate mass surveillance’

segments.body: Judge Sara Hill ruled that a Tulsa County sheriff’s deputy should have obtained a warrant before searching Flock Safety’s database for a woman’s license plate. She found no apparent reason for the search beyond the vehicle’s California plate and said evidence obtained afterwards must be suppressed.

segments.title: Broader privacy concerns
segments.body: Hill warned that passively cataloguing the movements of all vehicles over time and making that data available to police on demand raises constitutional concerns. The ruling does not set binding precedent. Local governments have moved to stop using the system, and Senator Bernie Sanders has introduced a bill to bar federal agencies from using automated plate readers such as Flock.

content.headline: India blocks downloads of Jack Dorsey’s offline messaging app Bitchat
content.shortHeadline: India restricts access to offline messaging app
content.standfirst: Bitchat has disappeared from major app stores in India after a government order, months after authorities also sought action against its GitHub repositories. Digital-rights advocates say the latest block exceeds the law’s scope.

sources.originalTitle: Jack Dorsey’s Bitchat disappears from app stores in India after government order

segments.body: Bitchat, an open-source messaging app that uses Bluetooth mesh networking to send encrypted messages between nearby devices without internet or cellular service, is no longer available through Apple’s or Google’s Indian app stores, according to TechCrunch’s checks. Apple’s notice cited a government order under Section 69A of India’s Information Technology Act; the app remained available in Apple’s store outside India.

segments.title: Dispute over the order
segments.body: India’s earlier action against Bitchat’s GitHub repositories cited concerns that its design made communications hard to intercept and allowed it to work during internet shutdowns. The Internet Freedom Foundation called the latest block unconstitutional, arguing Section 69A does not permit blocking an app for that functionality. The order and the allegedly unlawful content behind it have not been made public. Google and the IT ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

content.headline: Dutch spy agency warns connected cars could expose occupants’ data
content.shortHeadline: Dutch agency warns smart cars may enable spying
content.standfirst: The AIVD says vehicle microphones, cameras, GPS and connected devices could provide data to state actors or other malicious parties. It advises against confidential conversations in or around cars, while not naming a country.

image.caption: A modern car with connected digital systems that can collect data about occupants and their surroundings.

sources.originalTitle: Tech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warn

segments.body: The Netherlands’ General Intelligence and Security Service says some modern vehicles can collect extensive information and that microphones and cameras may be technically activated remotely. It also warns that phones connected by Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or charging systems could expose data through a vehicle’s systems.

segments.title: Advice and context
segments.body: The AIVD recommends avoiding confidential conversations in or near vehicles and cautions against using cars with external cameras when travelling to sensitive locations. The agency did not identify a country in its warning. The article places it amid UK concerns about Chinese-made cars, but that context does not establish that the Dutch agency was referring to China.

content.headline: California laws require more data-centre disclosures and oversight
content.shortHeadline: California mandates new data-centre reporting
content.standfirst: Seven new laws will require some reporting on data-centre energy and water use, establish separate electricity rates and expand environmental review. Advocates welcome the move but say gaps in the rules will remain.

sources.originalTitle: Data centers are black boxes, but California wants to change that

segments.body: California Governor Gavin Newsom signed seven bills addressing data centres’ effects on electricity, water and local communities. One requires monthly energy-use reporting starting next year; other measures require water disclosures, direct regulators to develop separate power rates and make data centres subject to environmental review.

segments.title: Information still missing
segments.body: Researchers and advocates say data on data-centre water use has been difficult to obtain, making it hard to assess costs and impacts. The new rules leave gaps: some water disclosures are tied to permits or business licences rather than ongoing use. A researcher quoted in the report calls the legislation a step in the right direction, but says greater transparency is still needed to assess how facilities affect communities.

content.headline: Electric hydrofoil ferry offers a smoother ride on rivers and bays
content.shortHeadline: An electric hydrofoil ferry skims above the water
content.standfirst: Vessev’s VS-9 lifts its hull on submerged wings to reduce drag and smooth the ride. The company sees potential for short urban routes, though the design works best in relatively calm waters and remains at an early stage.

sources.originalTitle: Vessev built an electric ferry that almost flies

segments.body: The VS-9 is a 30-foot electric catamaran that uses wing-like foils beneath its hull to lift the boat as it gains speed. Computer-controlled flaps help stabilise it. On a short ride in New York, a TechCrunch reporter found the transition subtle, describing the experience as more like a sports car than flight.

segments.title: Where it may fit
segments.body: Lifting the hull can reduce drag, a potential advantage for an electric vessel where energy efficiency matters. The design is not suited to every route: waves above about 2.5 feet can hit the hull and reduce its smoothness and efficiency. Vessev is targeting transit, hotels and tour operators, but the boat ridden by the reporter was a one-off and the company plans to build more.

content.headline: OpenAI safety-report writer quits, saying company culture is ‘broken’
content.shortHeadline: OpenAI safety lead quits over ‘broken’ culture
content.standfirst: David Robinson, who worked on safety reports for major product launches, says rapid development and trial-and-error safeguards leave firms unprepared for failures. OpenAI says it is strengthening testing, security and monitoring.

image.caption: OpenAI safety-report writer David Robinson, who resigned and criticised the company’s culture.

sources.originalTitle: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’
OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’
An OpenAI safety employee has quit and is sounding the alarm

segments.body: David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports accompanying OpenAI product releases, has resigned and criticised the company’s culture. He argues the industry’s rapid launch cycles and reliance on fixing problems after they appear are inadequate as systems become more capable. OpenAI says it pauses training or holds back models when needed and is improving safety practices.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch’s account adds Robinson’s call for AI firms to adopt safeguards modelled on nuclear plants and busy airports, and his criticism that he had not encountered colleagues with experience in those safety-critical fields.

segments.title: A debate beyond rules
segments.body: Robinson argues that safety requires more than new rules: companies need outside expertise and a culture that allows time for careful planning. His comments follow other departures and warnings from AI researchers. These are attributed concerns from industry insiders, not proof that the catastrophic scenarios they fear will occur.

perspectives.body: The Verge places Robinson among a wider group of researchers and safety workers who have left prominent AI companies and publicly warned about development practices.

content.headline: Google restricts its advanced AI model to vetted cybersecurity testers
content.shortHeadline: Google limits powerful AI model to vetted testers
content.standfirst: Google says Gemini 4 Argon can find and fix software flaws, but is withholding it from the public while cybersecurity experts test it. The company says early access uncovered a flaw in hospital software that exposed sensitive data.

sources.originalTitle: Google rolls out new Gemini AI model but restricts access over safety concerns

segments.body: Google is making Gemini 4 Argon available only to a vetted group of cybersecurity experts, saying a phased release is needed for a model with advanced cyber capabilities. The company says Argon can identify and fix critical software flaws and that early testers found a flaw in software used by hospitals around the world that exposed sensitive personal information.

segments.title: A cautious rollout
segments.body: Google says the model is designed to refuse requests that could assist cyberattacks or the development of chemical, biological or nuclear weapons. It is also monitoring the model for signs it may act beyond users’ intentions. The company says it will collect feedback before deciding whether to make Argon more widely available; the claims about its capabilities and test results are Google’s own.

content.headline: AI chatbots can remove religious head coverings from images, tests find
content.shortHeadline: Chatbots remove hijabs in image-editing tests
content.standfirst: The Guardian tested four chatbots and found that some would remove a hijab from an AI-generated image, despite restrictions they described on altering real people’s appearance. The tests expose gaps in how platforms treat identity and consent.

image.caption: Illustration accompanying reporting on chatbot image-editing tests and religious head coverings.

sources.originalTitle: AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when prompted

segments.body: In tests by The Guardian, ChatGPT and Grok complied with a request to remove a hijab from an AI-generated image. Gemini initially refused, but produced an unveiled image after being asked to make the woman look more “western”. Claude said it would not alter a real woman’s image in this way, though it does not offer image editing.

segments.title: A boundary with consequences
segments.body: The reporting followed the circulation of an altered image of a Muslim woman by a French far-right politician. The article says it was unclear which software was used to edit that image or who made the alteration. Researchers and advocates warn that removing religious dress can harm or misrepresent people, even without nudity, while the chatbot tests point to inconsistent safeguards around consent and identity.

content.headline: AI tools can speed up political influence operations, experts warn
content.shortHeadline: AI could speed political influence operations
content.standfirst: Anthropic says an operation targeting Malaysian voters used Claude to help create fake accounts, a news site and fabricated documents. Researchers say AI can make disinformation cheaper and more tailored, though it still needs channels to reach people.

image.caption: A composite of AI-generated images and posts discussed in reporting on political influence operations.

sources.originalTitle: How AI could ‘supercharge’ election risks across south-east Asia

segments.body: Anthropic reported that actors used Claude to help build a political influence operation aimed at Malaysian voters, including a network of about 1,000 X accounts, a fake news outlet and fabricated documents. The operation drew on electoral and census data to target political and social divisions. Anthropic says it disrupted the activity; the article does not describe the attempt as successful.

segments.title: Speed is not reach
segments.body: Former Meta elections policy director Katie Harbath says AI can make the production of personalised content quicker and cheaper, but operators still need a way to distribute it. Researchers cited in the report point to earlier uses of AI-generated political comments and images in the region, including content that reinforced existing tensions.

content.headline: Apple plans clearer consent before Mac apps get full disk access
content.shortHeadline: Apple to make Mac full-disk access more explicit
content.standfirst: Apple says it will require clearer user action before apps receive full disk access, which can expose files, messages, mail and browsing history. The move follows questions about desktop AI agents, though the specific reports involved are disputed.

sources.originalTitle: Apple will limit Mac disk access as AI agents ‘substantially’ increase risk
Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents

segments.body: Apple says it will add controls so that Mac users must take “very explicit” action to grant an app full disk access, a permission that can reach files, messages, mail and browsing history. The company says some developers use the permission in ways that could put users at risk, and that more capable AI agents heighten those risks.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch clarifies that Apple’s announcement concerns informed consent, not a new limit on what the permission can access; it also notes that Meta disputed a journalist’s claim that Muse had read private messages without permission.

segments.title: Permission and privacy
segments.body: The change follows a report by journalist Jason Aten that Meta’s Muse appeared to know the contents of his messages; Meta said access required enabling both Full Disk Access and a Messages connector. Apple has not said when the new controls will arrive. Its announcement addresses user consent but does not establish whether Muse accessed Aten’s messages without permission.

content.headline: Bank of England governor warns AI investment could unsettle markets
content.shortHeadline: Bailey warns AI bets could bring market shocks
content.standfirst: Andrew Bailey says the scale of investment and high expectations around AI could lead to a correction in company valuations. He sees potential economic benefits too, but says markets and financial systems must be prepared for losses.

image.caption: Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey speaking about AI risks, including deepfakes.

sources.originalTitle: AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns
AI boom could trigger market shocks, Bank of England boss warns

segments.body: Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey says the central bank is watching the money flowing into AI “very carefully”. He warned that some companies are priced as if they will all succeed, and that a correction in asset prices could create shocks. He compared the uncertainty to earlier technology shifts in which once-dominant companies lost their positions.

segments.title: Risks beyond valuation
segments.body: Bailey also cited potential AI-enabled cyberattacks and deepfakes, while saying the technology could help support the work of policymakers. His warning came amid high government borrowing costs, but the report does not identify AI investment as the specific trigger for that day’s bond-market movements. The central bank’s concern is whether the financial system can withstand shocks if expectations fail to materialise.

perspectives.body: The BBC account adds the bond-market context and Bailey’s view that AI could assist the Monetary Policy Committee’s work without taking decisions itself.

content.headline: AI hallucinations leave workers correcting customers’ false claims
content.shortHeadline: Workers say customers trust AI over real expertise
content.standfirst: Restaurant staff, park rangers and childcare workers describe customers treating chatbots as authoritative, even when advice is wrong. Their accounts show how AI errors can affect real interactions, from allergy warnings to impossible itineraries.

sources.originalTitle: AI hallucinations are making entitled customers even worse

segments.body: Workers interviewed by The Verge say some customers cite ChatGPT to challenge restaurant staff about allergens or ask for wines that are not on the menu. A river ranger describes visitors arriving with AI-generated itineraries that include nonexistent campsites or routes that cannot be travelled as suggested.

segments.title: A human handoff
segments.body: A childcare worker also describes parents relying on chatbot advice about a child’s sleep schedule despite concerns raised by staff. The article includes a restaurant manager’s suspicion that an AI agent may have made impractical event requests, which she could not verify. The accounts illustrate reported problems, not a measure of how often AI errors occur.
